entities.name: Pierre de Foix, le vieux
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pierre de Foix the Elder (1386–1464), a scion of the powerful House of Foix, emerged as a pivotal figure in the late Western Schism and the subsequent re-establishment of papal authority in France. Elevated to cardinal by the Avignon Antipope Benedict XIII in 1409 at the remarkably young age of 23, his career spanned decades of ecclesiastical and political maneuvering, primarily centered in the Comtat Venaissin and the former papal seat of Avignon. His significance lies in his enduring influence as a papal legate, navigating the complex allegiances of French nobility and contributing to the eventual reunification of the Church under a single Roman pontiff, albeit from a position initially hostile to Rome.

His early cardinalate under Benedict XIII cemented his initial loyalty to the Avignon line, a stance complicated by the Council of Constance's deposition of Benedict in 1417. Despite this, Pierre de Foix gradually transitioned his allegiance to the Roman papacy, serving as papal legate in Avignon from 1433 until his death. In this capacity, he wielded immense temporal and spiritual power, administering the Comtat Venaissin, negotiating with French monarchs like Charles VII, and actively participating in the Council of Basel. He was instrumental in suppressing local unrest and maintaining the papal presence in a region increasingly asserting its Gallican liberties, even hosting Pope Eugene IV briefly in Avignon in 1436.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pierre de Foix played a crucial role in stabilizing papal authority in Southern France after the Western Schism, ensuring the continued papal possession of the Comtat Venaissin and reconciling French loyalties to the unified Roman papacy.
